title: AI now writes real code. Here is what it looks like.
deck: Researchers looked at AI-written code in real projects. It runs longer, flags more high-risk spots, and gets rewritten more.
editor_notes: The 88 of 100 hand check is read as: of 100 sampled positives, 88 were truly AI code (paper says TP=88/100). Confirm wording against the paper.
'Changed again within 90 days' reads the Table 17 row 'Line churned 90 days' as the average per commit. Confirm.
Paper has a v3 (1 Jul 2026). This story is based on v2 and carries the 'based on v2' flag until a human reads v3.

reuse.text: The increased size of AI-generated code is not driven by additional comments, but by expanded code structures

intro.note: Intro says AI-assisted programming is becoming mainstream.

prior.note: Earlier studies used small, controlled settings.

cards.headline: AI writes code now. Is it any good?

sentences.t: Programmers now let AI write parts of the apps you use.
So here is a fair question.
Does AI code look different from code written by people?

cards.headline: Where do you look for the answer?

sentences.t: Earlier studies used small tests built in a lab.
This team went to real projects on GitHub instead.
GitHub is a site where programmers share and save their code.
They found 12,749 saves of code where AI helped.
A save point, called a commit, comes with a short note from the programmer.
Those saves touched 19,816 files.
In a hand check of 100 samples, 88 were truly AI code.

cards.headline: A fair test needs fair partners

sentences.t: They also gathered 36,467 files written by people.
Those human files were matched to the AI files to cancel out project quirks.
The average AI file has 256.57 lines. The average human file has 192.68.
That is 33% longer.

visual.title: Lines per file, average
visual.alt: Two bars. The AI bar, 256.57 lines, is longer than the human bar, 192.68 lines.
visual.caption: Rebuilt from the paper's numbers. Not a copy of any paper figure.

sentences.t: Comments make up 18.01% of AI code and 17.96% of human code.
Blank lines are 15.15% of AI code and 13.46% of human code.
So the extra length is plain code, not extra notes.

quote.text: The increased size of AI-generated code is not driven by additional comments, but by expanded code structures

cards.headline: Longer is not worse. But is it safer?

sentences.t: A long file can still be a good file.
So the team ran a code scanner over everything.
A scanner flags spots that might hide a bug or a security hole.
For equal amounts of code, the scanner raised 12.81 flags on AI code and 11.58 on human code.
Critical flags were rarer in AI code: 0.042 against 0.052.

visual.title: Scanner flags for equal amounts of code
visual.alt: Four pairs of bars. For all flags the two are close. For critical, AI is slightly lower. For high risk and medium risk, AI is higher.
visual.caption: Each pair has its own scale. Rebuilt from the paper's numbers.

sentences.t: High-risk flags show up 2.01 times as often in AI code.
Medium-risk flags also rise, from 0.182 to 0.282.
Only the critical flags go the other way.

cards.headline: Does that hold for every language?

sentences.t: An average can hide a split.
Let us look inside the average.

cards.headline: Contested: the average hides a split

sentences.t: Headline: AI code has 2.01 times the high-risk flags.
In JavaScript it is 4.02 against 1.14 for people.
In TypeScript it flips: 0.078 against 0.794.
The paper itself calls the effect language-dependent.

contested.explain: The single headline number mixes languages that move in opposite directions. Read it as a pattern in some languages, not a law.

sentences.t: The average AI commit changes 24.70 lines. A human commit changes 152.02.
But within 90 days, AI commits see 3.19 lines changed again, against 0.275 for human commits.
That is 11.6 times as much.

visual.title: Lines changed per commit, average
visual.alt: Two pairs of bars. In the commit, AI changes far fewer lines than people. Changed again later, AI is far higher.
visual.caption: Each pair has its own scale. Rebuilt from the paper's numbers.

sentences.t: Picture each save as a stone dropped in a pond.
The ripples are the later edits that follow.

visual.name: ripple-after-commit
visual.title: Ripples after a save
visual.alt: A small stone drops into water and rings spread outward, showing later edits that follow a save.
visual.caption: Animation, no numbers. Small drop with big ripples stands for the AI pattern in the last card.

sentences.t: Secrets like API keys should never sit inside code.
For equal amounts of code, AI code hard-codes keys or tokens at a rate of 0.194, against 0.098 for people.
That is 1.98 times as often.
People hard-code more passwords: 1.02 against 0.703.
Treat AI code like a fast helper's first draft.
Expect more length, a closer security read, and more rewrites.
This is a preprint, so other experts have not yet reviewed it.
It shows patterns across many projects. It does not prove that AI caused them.
